section.heading: Scope.
section.text: This chapter applies to a pharmacy licensed in Maryland engaging in:

para.text: Compounding or mixing sterile prescription solutions or suspensions to be administered by:
Injection or infusion;
Irrigations for internal body cavities;
Ophthalmic;
Pulmonary inhalation;
Baths and soaks for live organs and tissues; or
Implant routes;

Compounding of Hazardous Drugs when U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) General Chapter 797 Pharmaceutical Compounding––Sterile Preparations states that U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) Chapter 800 Hazardous Drugs––Handling in Healthcare Settings would apply; and

Compounding of radiopharmaceuticals, when U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) General Chapter 797 Pharmaceutical Compounding––Sterile Preparations states that USP Chapter 825 Radiopharmaceuticals––Preparation, Compounding, Dispensing, and Repackaging would apply.

section.heading: Incorporation by Reference.
section.text: In this chapter, the following documents are incorporated by reference:

para.text: U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) General Chapter 797 Pharmaceutical Compounding—Sterile Preparations (USP 797 Standards), which has been incorporated by reference in 21 U.S.C. §353a (as amended);
U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) General Chapter 800 Hazardous Drugs––Handling in Healthcare Settings (USP 800 Standards), which has been incorporated by reference in 21 U.S.C. §353a (as amended); and
U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) Chapter 825 Radiopharmaceuticals—Preparation, Compounding, Dispensing, and Repackaging, which has been incorporated by reference in 21 U.S.C. §353a (as amended).
In this chapter, the following terms have the meanings indicated.
Terms Defined.
Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient.

“Active pharmaceutical ingredient” means any substance or mixture of substances intended to be used in the compounding of a preparation, thereby becoming the active ingredient in that preparation, and furnishing pharmacological activity or other direct effect in:
The diagnosis;
The cure;
The mitigation;
The treatment;
The prevention of disease in humans and animals; or
How the structure and function of the body is affected.
“Active pharmaceutical ingredient” does not include a conventionally manufactured drug product that is typically manufactured from an active pharmaceutical ingredient.
“Adverse event” means:
Any adverse patient outcome related to the sterile compounding process; or
Evidence of environmental contamination, including microbial contamination above the threshold set forth in USP 797 Standards.

“Anteroom” means an International Standards Organization Class 8 or cleaner room with fixed walls and doors where personnel hand hygiene, garbing procedures, and other activities that generate high particulate levels may be performed. The anteroom is the transition room between the unclassified area of the facility and the buffer room.
Batch.

“Batch” means a preparation compounded in advance of receipt of a prescription, or a preparation compounded in a supply that will be used on more than one dispensing to a patient or patients or any preparation compounded in excess of the filling of an individual prescription.
“Batch” includes a limited quantity of identical preparations compounded in a single, discrete process, by the same individuals, carried out during one limited time period.
“Beyond-use date” means the date, or hour and the date, after which a CSP must not be used, stored, or transported. The date is determined from the date and time the preparation is compounded.
“Biological safety cabinet” means a ventilated containment unit:
Suitable for work involving agents that pose higher risk of exposure to operators during compounding; and
Used when there is a need for protection of the preparation, personnel, and environment.

“Buffer room” means an International Standards Organization Class 7 or cleaner room with fixed walls and doors where primary engineering controls that generate and maintain an International Standards Organization Class 5 environment are physically located. The buffer room may only be accessed through the anteroom or another buffer room.
“Classified area” means an area that maintains an air quality classification based on the ISO standards required by US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards.
“Cleanroom suite” means a classified area that consists of both an anteroom and a buffer room.

“Closed-system drug-transfer device” means a drug-transfer device that mechanically prohibits the transfer of environmental contaminants into the system and the escape of hazardous drugs or vapor concentrations outside of the system.

“Compounded sterile preparation (CSP)” means a medication preparation intended to be sterile that is created by combining, admixing, diluting, pooling, reconstituting, repackaging, assembling, or otherwise altering a drug product or bulk drug substance.

“Compounding” means the process of combining, admixing, diluting, pooling, reconstituting, repackaging, assembling, or otherwise altering a drug product or bulk drug substance to create a sterile preparation:
As the result of a practitioner’s prescription drug order or initiative based on the practitioner/patient relationship in the course of professional practice;
For the purpose of, or incidental to, research, teaching, or chemical analysis and not for the sale or dispensing of the drug or device; or
In anticipation of a prescription drug order based on routine, regularly observed prescribing patterns.

“Compounding aseptic isolator” means a type of restricted access barrier that uses high efficiency particulate air filtration to provide an ISO Class 5 unidirectional air environment designed for compounding of sterile non-hazardous drugs.

“Compounding aseptic containment isolator” means a type of restricted-access barrier that uses high efficiency particulate air filtration to provide an ISO Class 5 unidirectional air environment designed for the compounding of sterile hazardous drugs.
“Designee” means a public agency or private entity recognized by the Board to conduct sterile compounding inspections that is trained in:
USP 797 Standards;
FDA good manufacturing practices approved by the Board to conduct inspections of nonresident pharmacies that perform sterile compounding; or
Both §B(15)(a) and (b) of this regulation.
“Dynamic operating conditions” means conditions in the compounding area in which operating personnel are present and simulating or performing compounding activities.

“Expiration” means the time period during which a manufactured product is expected to remain stable, or retain its identity, strength, quality, and purity, when it is properly stored according to its labeled storage conditions.

“Hazardous drug” means a drug included on the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health list of antineoplastic and other hazardous drugs in healthcare settings, which are identified by at least one of the following six criteria:
Carcinogenicity;
Teratogenicity or developmental toxicity;
Reproductive toxicity in humans;
Organ toxicity at low dose in humans or animals;
Genotoxicity; or
New drugs that mimic existing hazardous drugs in structure or toxicity.
“Healthcare practitioner intermediary” means an entity or person that connects healthcare providers with patients, payers, or other relevant parties.

“High efficiency particulate air filtration” means a filtration system that has the ability to capture particles at its most penetrating particle size and removing 99.97 percent of particles at .03 micrometers.
“International Organization for Standardization class” means an air-quality classification from the International Organization for Standardization.

“Laminar airflow system” means a device or zone within a buffer room that provides an International Standards Organization Class 5 or better air quality environment for sterile compounding. The system provides a unidirectional high efficiency particulate air-filtered airflow.

“Laminar airflow workbench” means a device that is a type of laminar airflow system that provides an International Standards Organization Class 5 or better air quality environment for sterile compounding. The device provides a unidirectional high efficiency particulate air-filtered airflow.

“Media-fill test” means a simulation used to qualify processes and personnel engaged in sterile compounding to ensure that the processes and personnel are able to prepare compounding sterile preparations without contamination.

“National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health list” means the list maintained by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health of antineoplastic and other hazardous drugs used in healthcare.
“Parenteral” means routes of drug administration or fluid administration other than via the gastrointestinal tract.
“Pharmacist” means an individual who is licensed to practice pharmacy regardless of the location where the activities of practice are performed.
“Pharmacy” means an establishment in which prescription or nonprescription drugs or devices are compounded, dispensed, or distributed.
“Primary engineering control” means a device or zone that provides an International Standards Organization Class 5 air quality environment for sterile compounding.
“Pyrogen testing” means an analysis of sterile preparations for the presence of cell material from microbiological organisms in sufficient quantity to elicit a febrile reaction.

“Restricted-access barrier system” means an enclosure that provides high efficiency particulate air-filtered International Standards Organization Class 5 unidirectional air that allows for the ingress or egress, or both, of materials through defined openings that have been designed and validated to preclude the transfer of contamination, and that generally are not to be opened during operations.
“Secondary engineering control” means a space which provides a classified area where primary engineering controls are placed.
“Sterile” means free from viable microorganisms.

“Sterile compounding” means the process of combining, admixing, diluting, pooling, reconstituting, repackaging, assembling, or otherwise altering a drug product or bulk drug substance to create a preparation using aseptic techniques in accordance with US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards.
“Total parenteral nutrition” means providing nutritional needs by the parenteral route for a patient who is unable to ingest sufficient calories.
“USP 797 Standards” means standards set forth in the U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) General Chapter 797 Pharmaceutical Compounding — Sterile Preparations.
“US Pharmacopeia 800 Standards” means the standards set forth in US Pharmacopeia General Chapter 800 Hazardous Drugs––Handling in Healthcare Settings.
“US Pharmacopeia 825 Standards” means the standards set forth in US Pharmacopeia General Chapter 825 Radiopharmaceuticals––Preparation, Compounding, Dispensing, and Repackaging.

section.heading: General Requirements.
section.text: A licensed supervising pharmacist who has appropriate practical and didactic training in compounding sterile preparations, cleanroom technology, laminar flow technology, quality assurance techniques, and clinical application of intravenous drug therapy shall control and supervise the section of the pharmacy that prepares compounded sterile preparations and is responsible for, at a minimum, the following:

para.text: Preparation of compounded sterile preparations within the pharmacy or decentralized pharmacy;

Storage of materials pertinent to the preparation of compounded sterile preparations, including drugs, chemicals, and biologicals, and the establishment of specifications for procurement of the materials;
Labeling of containers of compounded sterile preparations compounded within or dispensed by the pharmacy;

Recording of transactions of the pharmacy as may be applicable to State and federal laws and regulations, as may be necessary to maintain accurate control over, and accountability for, pharmaceutical materials;
Overseeing an initial and ongoing training and competency program for all staff with duties within the cleanroom in accordance with US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards and Regulation .14 of this chapter;
Ensuring engineering controls and equipment utilized for compounding meet the US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards and Regulation .09 of this chapter;
Ensuring policies and procedures, provided in US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards and Regulation .12 of this chapter, are implemented, maintained, and reviewed on an annual basis; and
Overseeing a quality assurance and quality control program to monitor:
Adherence to policies and procedures;
Prevention and detection of errors and quality issues;
Investigation of complaints and reported adverse events; and
Corrective actions and recall programs.

section.heading: Special Handling, Packaging, Labeling, and Beyond Use Dating.

para.text: The pharmacy shall make available special handling and packaging materials to maintain container integrity and drug stability of the prepared prescription orders, including hazardous sterile preparations, during handling and administration to the patient including:
A reasonable effort to provide tamper-evident packaging on compounded sterile preparations;
Proper in-transit storage consistent with preparation labeling;

For medications not distributed to a Healthcare Practitioner Intermediary, the enclosure of information to inform the patient if the prescription is a temperature sensitive medication that is at risk for damage due to extreme hot or cold temperatures or moisture; and
Delivery to the patient within a reasonable time.
The dispensed container for any compounded sterile preparation shall include labeling according to State law and regulations, in addition to the following information:
The date of the preparation unless otherwise readily retrievable from prescription records;
Time prepared, if applicable;
The pertinent requirements for proper storage;
The name of the prescriber, unless in an inpatient hospital setting;
The name of the patient;
Directions for use;
The name of the base solution for infusion preparations;
The name and concentration or amount of active drugs contained in the final sterile preparation;

The name or identifying initials of the individual who prepared the compounded sterile preparation and the pharmacist who checked the compounded sterile preparation unless otherwise readily retrievable from prescription records;
The name, address, and telephone number of the pharmacy unless in an inpatient hospital facility;
The beyond-use date and time of the compounded sterile preparation, and if no time is stated, the time is presumed to be at 11:59 p.m. of the stated date;
Any ancillary and cautionary instructions as needed; and
A pertinent warning consistent with applicable federal and State law of the presence of hazardous drugs including instructions for safe handling and proper disposal.

A pharmacy compounding sterile preparations shall provide a 24-hour telephone number to allow its patients or other health care providers who may be administering its prescriptions to contact its pharmacists.
Beyond-use Dates.
A pharmacy shall use timeframes for beyond-use dates as determined by US Pharmacopeia 797 Category 1 or 2 Standards; and

Beyond-use dates greater than those set forth in US Pharmacopeia 797 Category 1 or 2 Standards shall comply with US Pharmacopeia 797 Category 3 Standards and appropriate reference materials cited in Regulation .16 of this chapter.
Patient Prescription Records.
The pharmacy shall maintain records of patient prescriptions.
Patient prescription records shall contain:
Available medical information consistent with prevailing pharmacy standards; and
The complete record of the formulations of the solutions that were compounded.
The pharmacy shall keep completed patient prescription records in a retrievable manner for at least 5 years, either:
At the inspection site; or
So as to be immediately retrievable by computer or other electronic means.
Compounded Sterile Preparations Records.
For a pharmacy preparing compounded sterile preparations, the following records shall be maintained for at least 5 years:
The training and competency evaluation of:
Pharmacy employees in sterile preparation procedures; and
Non-pharmacy employees responsible for the maintenance and cleaning of the cleanroom;
Refrigerator and freezer temperatures;
Incubator temperatures when in use;
Certification of the classified area, including ISO 5 workstations cleanrooms, and other controlled rooms, such as hazardous drug storage areas;
Other daily facility quality control logs specific to the pharmacy's policies and procedures, such as:
Cleaning logs for facilities and equipment;
Cleanroom pressures; and
Temperature and humidity;
Records documenting inspection for expired or recalled pharmaceutical preparations, components, or raw ingredients;
Trending of microbiological growth and actions taken for adverse trending;
Investigations, corrective actions, and preventative measures for any adverse event;
Certificates of analysis of active pharmaceutical ingredient components of compounded sterile preparations, and microbial growth;
Safety data sheets of active pharmaceutical ingredients utilized in the process of sterile compounding and other chemicals and cleaning agents utilized in the cleanroom suite;
Documentation of recalls initiated by the pharmacy of compounded sterile products;
Compounding and preparation records, including:
Worksheets;
Processing checklists;
Procedure sign-off forms; and
Final check logs;

Master formulation record as described by US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards for all compounded sterile preparations prepared from nonsterile ingredients or compounded sterile preparations prepared for more than one patient; and
The results and documentation of applicable end product sterilization, testing, and validation.

In addition to the records requirement in §B(1) of this regulation, for batch compounded sterile preparations, a pharmacy compounding sterile batch preparations for future use shall have records indicating the:
Drug and ingredient names;
Lot numbers;
Expiration dates of components;
Drug/diluent amounts;
Assigned beyond-use dates; and
Date on which the compounded sterile batch preparations were prepared.
A pharmacy may prepare batched sterile preparations for future use before receiving a valid written prescription or medication order.
Batch preparation of specific compounded sterile preparations is acceptable if the pharmacy:

Compounds limited quantities based on a documented history of valid prescriptions or physician orders that have been generated solely within an established professional prescriber-patient-pharmacist relationship; and
Maintains the prescription on file for each compounded sterile preparation dispensed.
Batch preparation labeling shall meet the requirements of Regulation .06 of this chapter.
Record keeping of batch preparations shall meet the requirements of Regulation .07 of this chapter.
Classified Area.
The pharmacy shall have a classified area that meets USP 797, 800, or 825 Standards, as applicable.
The pharmacy shall ensure that the classified area is:
Accessible only to designated personnel; and
Used only for the preparation of compounded sterile preparations, or other tasks that require a classified area.
The pharmacy shall ensure that the classified area is:
Structurally isolated from other areas within the pharmacy by means of restricted entry or access; and
Air conditioned to maintain the temperature and humidity of the classified area according to USP 797 Standards.
If compounding occurs outside of a cleanroom, the area and procedures shall meet US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards for a segregated compounding area or for immediate use administration.
Buffer Room. The pharmacy shall ensure that the buffer room in the classified area:
Meets USP 797 Standards for design and USP 797 Standards for performance criteria quality for buffer rooms;
Contains no sinks or floor drains;
Contains work surfaces constructed of smooth, impervious materials, such as stainless steel or molded plastic, so that the work surfaces may be readily cleaned and sanitized;
If hazardous drugs are used in compounded preparations, contains room or rooms equipped with special pressurization requirements consistent with USP 797 and 800 Standards;
Has in place appropriate environmental engineering control devices capable of maintaining USP 797 Standards for air-quality during routine operations and under dynamic operating conditions; and
Contains the following equipment:
Primary engineering controls validated to maintain International Standards Organization (ISO) Class 5 compounding environment during routine operations and under dynamic operating conditions;
Waste containers that are approved by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) for used needles and syringes, and for hazardous drug waste; and
Ancillary supplies required for proper compounding.
Anteroom. The pharmacy shall ensure that the anteroom in the classified area:
Meets USP 797 Standards for design and USP 797 performance criteria quality standards for anterooms; and
Contains the following equipment:
A sink with hot and cold running water:
At least a meter away from a primary engineering control within a segregated compounding area; or
If outside the cleanroom suite, the pharmacy shall have a policy and procedure on how to maintain hand hygiene while entering the cleanroom and donning protective garb;
Waste containers; and
An eyewash station or sink design suitable for flushing an eye injury.
The pharmacy shall provide at least the following equipment that is maintained in working order:
Adequate refrigerator and freezer space (if applicable);
A sink for hand hygiene and if applicable, cleaning equipment;
Appropriate waste containers for:
Used needles and syringes; and
Hazardous drug waste including disposable personal protective equipment used in its preparation, if applicable;
Primary engineering controls that meet USP 797 Standards, dedicated for products other than hazardous drugs;

If applicable to types of preparations compounded, biological safety cabinet, or compounding aseptic containment isolator that meets USP 797 Standards, dedicated for use with hazardous or radiopharmaceutical sterile preparations;
Appropriate filters and filtration equipment; and
A dedicated space or equipment for light/dark field examination.
All equipment, devices, and monitoring tools utilized in the sterile compounding process shall be:
Maintained in working order;
Calibrated; and
Certified, where appropriate.

section.heading: Minimum Requirements for Supplies.
section.text: A pharmacy engaging in compounding sterile preparations shall maintain adequate stock levels of the following supplies according to USP 797 Standards, including but not limited to:

para.text: Garb for sterile compounding including:
Sterile gloves;
Masks;
Non-shedding gowns;
Shoe covers;
Hair covers;
Beard covers; and
Other garb and personal protective equipment for handling hazardous drugs as required per US Pharmacopeia 800 Standards;
Disposable syringes and needles in necessary sizes;
Cleaning agents as specified in USP 797 Standards including:
Disinfectant and sporicidal cleaning agents; and
Water, if utilized as part of the primary engineering control cleaning process, such as for rinsing surfaces or diluting cleaning agents, which shall be sterile;
Disposable lint free towels;
Hand washing materials, including:
Nail picks;
Antimicrobial skin cleanser; and
Alcohol-based hand rub;
Sesventyt at percent sterile isopropyl or ethyl alcohol;
Supplies necessary for the aseptic preparation of compounded sterile preparations;
A hazardous waste spill kit, if applicable; and
Closed system vial transfer devices (CSTD), as required for hazardous compounding, if applicable.

section.heading: Minimum Requirements for Policies and Procedures.

para.text: The pharmacy shall ensure that a supervising pharmacist shall maintain a policy and procedure manual, reviewed annually, that sets forth in detail the pharmacy’s standard operating procedures with regard to compounding sterile preparations.
The pharmacy shall ensure that the policy and procedure manual that sets forth the standard operating procedures with regard to compounding sterile preparations is implemented and adhered to.
The policy and procedure manual shall include policies and procedures governing the following:
A risk-management program which includes documentation of outcomes including, but not limited to:
Environmental excursions;
Adverse drug reactions;
Preparation contamination; and
Recalls of compounded sterile preparations prepared by the pharmacy.
Security measures ensuring that the premises where sterile compounded preparations are stored and prepared are secured, to prevent access by unauthorized personnel;
Equipment including, but not limited to:
Procedures for use;
Documentation of appropriate certifications; and
Documentation of appropriate calibration and preventive maintenance if applicable;
Sanitation and cleaning standards and procedures;
Maintenance and availability of reference materials as set forth in Regulation .16 of this chapter;
Information concerning drug:
Preparation;
Storage and handling;
Dispensing;
Labeling;
Beyond-use dating;
Release testing and verification;
Delivery;
Destruction;
Recalls; and
Returns;
Patient record keeping as set forth in Regulation .07 of this chapter;
Facility and equipment control monitoring as set forth in Regulation .07 of this chapter;
Facility certification and viable testing program, as described by US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards;
Handling, dispensing, and documentation of investigational drugs;
A quality assurance program;
Training verification procedures, including:
Gloved thumb and fingertip sampling;
Visual observation for adherence to aseptic technique; and
Media-fill testing with post gloved fingertip and thumb, and surface sampling;
Description of appropriate garb donning and doffing processes;
Conduct guidelines for personnel in the controlled areas;
Personnel responsibilities including:
Pharmacists who are not physically involved in the compounding process;
Compounding staff; and
Cleaning and maintenance staff who have access to the cleanroom;
Patient education, unless in an inpatient setting;
Protocols and procedures to maintain the integrity of the cleanroom suite and the primary engineering controls;
Handling of hazardous drugs as per US Pharmacopeia 800 Standards, if applicable, including:
Utilizing the proper equipment and supplies;
A statement that compounding shall be conducted within a properly certified biological safety cabinet or compounding aseptic containment isolator;
Proper use of personal protective equipment; and
Proper techniques to prevent both contamination of the preparation and chemical exposure of the individual preparing the medication;
Segregation of biological and hazardous material from other compounding activities to prevent cross-contamination, if applicable;
The disposal of infectious materials or materials containing hazardous drugs or waste, as per USP 800 Standards, if applicable;
Written documentation of policy and procedure changes based on data gathered from quality assurance evaluations; and
Assurance of the sterility and stability of compounded sterile preparations including end-product testing and sterilization, if applicable.

section.heading: Cleanroom Garbing.
section.text: When compounding sterile preparations, individuals shall comply with the following standards:

para.text: Sequencing of garbing that complies with USP 797 and 800 Standards, as applicable;
Thorough handwashing before gowning;
Wearing clean room garb inside the designated area at all times, which consists of:
A non-shedding coverall or gown;
Head and facial hair covers;
A face mask;
Shoe covers; and
Other personal protective equipment required for the handling and preparation of hazardous drugs, in accordance with US Pharmacopeia 800 Standards;
Cleanroom garb, with the exception of sterile gloves, shall be donned and removed outside the designated cleanroom area;
Personal protective equipment and garb required for the handling and preparation of hazardous drugs shall be removed, in accordance with US Pharmacopeia 800 Standards;
All jewelry that can be physically removed, shall be removed;
Sterile powder-free gloves are required;
Make-up, cosmetic lotions, creams, ointments, false nails, and other cosmetic accessories may not be worn in the cleanroom; and
Nails shall be natural and short, not extending past the nail bed.

section.heading: Training of Staff, Patient, and Caregiver.

para.text: The pharmacy shall make counseling available to the patient or primary caregiver, or both, concerning:
Proper use of compounded sterile preparations and related supplies dispensed by the pharmacy;
Signs of contamination or other issues seen in CSPs; and
Proper disposal of:
Excess medications;
Biohazards;
Sharps; and
Hazardous drug waste.

The pharmacy shall ensure that pharmacy personnel engaging in compounding sterile preparations are trained and demonstrate competence in the safe handling and compounding of sterile preparations, including hazardous drugs, if applicable.
The pharmacy shall maintain records of training and demonstrated competence for individual employees for 5 years.
The pharmacy shall ensure the continuing competence of pharmacy personnel engaged in compounding sterile preparations.
A pharmacy that compounds sterile preparations shall comply with the following training requirements:

The pharmacy shall establish and follow a written program of annual training and performance evaluation designed to ensure that individuals working in the designated area have the knowledge and skills necessary to perform the assigned tasks properly and include at least the following:
Aseptic technique with gloved fingertip and thumb sampling, and media-fill testing with post gloved thumb and fingertip and surface sampling at a minimum frequency defined by USP 797 Standards;
Pharmaceutical calculations and terminology;
Sterile compounding documentation process;
Quality assurance procedures;
Aseptic preparation procedures, including principles of unidirectional airflow;
Proper hand cleansing, gowning, and gloving techniques;
General conduct within the controlled area;
Cleaning, sanitizing, and maintaining:
Equipment used in the classified area; and
The cleanroom suite;
Sterilization techniques, if applicable;
Container and closure system selection; and
Identifying and reporting problems, failures, and errors to designated individuals.
Individuals assigned to the classified area shall successfully complete practical skills training in aseptic technique and aseptic area practices prior to compounding medication for patients.
Evaluations shall include:
Written testing;
Observation for adherence to aseptic technique and aseptic area policies and procedures; and
Media-fill testing with gloved fingertip and thumb sampling, and surface sampling as set forth in §E(1)(a) of this regulation.

A pharmacy with only one pharmacist performing compounding shall establish and maintain training and competencies through a third party who is competent in the requirements set forth in this chapter and US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards.

Ensuring that all individuals who enter the cleanroom for cleaning, maintenance, or any other reason shall, at a minimum, have demonstrated competence and understanding of appropriate garbing, hand hygiene, conduct, and duties within the cleanroom.
Ensuring that all individuals responsible for handling, storing, packing, and transporting of CSPs shall be trained in duties associated with their position.
The completion, upon initial hire, evaluations as set forth in §E(1) of this regulation, including three passing consecutive gloved fingertip and thumb samplings.

section.heading: Quality Assurance.
section.text: The pharmacy shall ensure that the CSP retains its potency and sterility throughout the assigned beyond-use date through a written quality assurance program that includes:

para.text: A reasonable effort by the pharmacist to assure that compounded sterile preparations shall be kept under appropriate controlled conditions before dispensing, during transport, and at the location of use by providing adequate labeling and verbal or written instructions regarding proper storage and administration, as set forth by the product manufacturer and established standards and literature, with each compounded sterile preparation dispensed;
The sterile compounding process, distribution, storage, administration, and directions for use for each type of preparation dispensed;
Primary engineering controls certification by a trained and qualified operator, according to US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards;
Secondary engineering control certification by a trained and qualified operator according to US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards;
Environmental sampling for microbial organisms is performed according to methods and schedules specified by US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards;
Trending of microbial growth observed during viable testing;

section.heading: Reference Library.
section.text: Minimum reference materials in a pharmacy shall include:

para.text: United States Pharmacopeia, General Chapter 797 Pharmaceutical Compounding—Sterile Preparations;

United States Pharmacopeia, General Chapter 825 Radiopharmaceuticals––Preparation, Compounding, Dispensing, and Repackaging;
Other applicable reference materials in order to perform sterile compounding;
Reference materials containing drug stability and compatibility data;
Reference materials concerning drug interactions and incompatibility; and
Reference materials containing drug dosing for veterinary patients, if applicable.
The Board shall inspect pharmacies located in Maryland at least annually.
The pharmacy shall provide as part of the inspection process:
Documents, reports, and information required in accordance with this chapter; and
Any other information requested to ensure compliance with USP 797 Standards.
Non-resident Pharmacies. Within 90 days before the date of application, inspections may be conducted by:
A designee of the Board;
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration; or
Another appropriate state entity which indicates compliance with USP 797 Standards.
The Board or designee shall inspect nonresident pharmacies upon initial application and upon renewal.
The Board may inspect a pharmacy at any time to:
Verify compliance with permit requirements; or
Investigate a complaint.

The Board may reference guidance documents issued by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) when inspecting and reviewing compounding practices not specifically outlined in this chapter or a chapter of US Pharmacopeia.
Document and perform routine testing as required by US Pharmacopeia 797 Standards for the appropriate categories of sterile compounded preparations; and
Report to the Board within 5 calendar days:
Adverse events that have been discovered including corrective actions taken or proposed;
Deficiencies related to the sterile compounding process;
Disciplinary actions in other states or by other state agencies;
Changes in accreditation status;
Disciplinary actions taken against a pharmacist or technician who is an owner, operator, or employee of the pharmacy; and
Disciplinary actions taken against any other permit, or any other authorization, held by the pharmacy permit holder.

section.heading: Office Use.
section.text: Unless otherwise authorized, a person that prepares and distributes sterile compounded medications for office use into, out of, or within the State shall hold:

para.text: A manufacturer’s permit or other registration as designated by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to ensure the safety of sterile compounded medications for office use; and
If applicable, a wholesale distributor’s permit, issued by the Board under Health Occupations Article, Title 12, Subtitle 6C, Annotated Code of Maryland.

para.text: This regulation governs the requirements for any meeting of a local board of education (local board). A local board shall comply with the rules generally adopted by deliberative bodies for their governance to ensure that all meetings are conducted in an open and transparent manner and as required by this Chapter.
Terms Defined. In this chapter, the following terms have the meaning indicated.

“Exceptional circumstances” means a temporary, unexpected event that makes an in-person meeting unfeasible or unsafe, such as a State or local government-declared public health emergency, severe weather event that closes schools and government offices, or an infrastructure failure that renders the designated meeting location unusable.
“In-person meeting” means the physical gathering of a quorum of a local board in a location to conduct public business.

“Open session” means a meeting or part of a meeting of the local board that is open to the public as required by the Maryland Open Meetings Act, General Provisions Article, Title 3, Annotated Code of Maryland.
“Regularly scheduled business meeting” means a recurring, pre-announced gathering of a quorum of the local board, conducted under a formal agenda for the purpose of conducting regular business.
“Special meetings” means any non-regularly scheduled meeting of a local board that is typically called to address urgent or specific matters that arise between regular meetings.
Requirements for Regularly Scheduled Business Meetings.

In-Person Meetings Required. A local board shall meet in person for a monthly regularly scheduled business meeting that includes an open session. The open session in-person meeting requirement does not apply to committees and task forces of the local board.
Public Observation. Regularly scheduled business meetings shall be held in a physical location that:
Admits the public;
Is reasonably accessible to individuals who wish to attend; and
Permits the public to observe and hear the meeting.
Hybrid Meetings. Board members may participate remotely by video or telephone conference.
Virtual Meetings — Limited Exception.
A local board may only meet virtually for a regularly scheduled business meeting under exceptional circumstances or special meetings as defined in §B of this regulation.
A local board shall meet the notice, access, and transparency requirements of Maryland’s Open Meetings Act.

Closed Session. This regulation permits a local board to meet virtually when convening in closed session, consistent with the requirements of the Maryland Open Meetings Act, General Provisions Article, Title 3, Annotated Code of Maryland.
Public Comment.
Opportunity for Public Comment. The local board shall permit a period during at least one of its regularly scheduled business meetings each month to hear comments from members of the public.
Adoption of Policy. The local board shall adopt a written policy regarding the process, rules, and procedures for public comment, which shall include:
The rules for registering to speak;
Any reasonable limitations on the time allotted to each speaker; and
The subject matter that may be addressed during the public comment period.
The local board shall make its public comment policy readily available to the public on its official website.
Motions and Resolutions.
A motion or resolution may not be declared adopted without the concurrence of a majority of the members of the local board.

A majority of members of the local board consists of three members when the board consists of five, four members when the board consists of six or seven, and five members when the board consists of eight or nine.

para.text: Each local school system shall provide a coordinated program of pupil services for all students which shall include but not be limited to:
School counseling;
Pupil personnel;
School psychology;
Health services; and
School Social Work.
The Pupil Services Program shall:
Focus on supporting student wellness, including physical, mental and behavioral health; and
Support social and emotional development to facilitate the academic achievement and career development of all students..
Each local school system shall develop and implement a plan to determine the Pupil Services Program needs of students.
Each local school system shall define, develop, implement, and evaluate its Pupil Services Program. The Pupil Services Program may:
Use preventive and remedial approaches to meet student needs; and
Include alternative and supplemental programs for students at risk.
Each local school system shall provide a Pupil Services Program Manual and a School Counseling Program Manual for the elementary and secondary schools under its jurisdiction. The following apply:
The Pupil Services Program Manual shall include:
The objectives of the Pupil Services Program set forth in §§A—E;
A pupil services philosophy;
Local goals and subgoals related to each of the goals established as part of the Pupil Services Program;
Procedures;
Program activities; and
A procedure for an annual evaluation of the Pupil Services Program;
The School Counseling Program Manual shall include:
Measurable student performance objectives that relate to each of the goals and subgoals established as part of the School Counseling Program in Regulation .02B of this chapter; and
A procedure for an annual evaluation of the extent to which student performance objectives are being attained.
The following procedures shall apply to the certification and program services:

Certification. By September 1, 1988, each local superintendent of schools shall certify to the State Superintendent of Schools that the Pupil Services Program meets, at a minimum, the requirements set forth in this regulation.
Program Reviews.
The State Department of Education shall implement a procedure for conducting periodic reviews of local school system Pupil Services Programs by September 1, 1988.
The purpose of the reviews is to identify, on a regular basis, the program and professional development needs that exist in pupil services.

Individuals providing services to students in the coordinated program of Pupil Services shall meet the State Certification requirements set forth in COMAR 13A.12.03, except nurses who shall meet the requirements set forth in Health Occupations Article, Title 8, Subtitle 3, Annotated Code of Maryland.
The School Social Worker Program is a program that:
Promotes student academic success and well-being;
Enhances awareness of mental health and promotes positive, healthy behaviors;
Provides school-based prevention and universal and targeted interventions for students with mental health and behavioral health concerns;
Is aligned with school system goals and objectives;
Is an integral component of the school’s program and mission;
Addresses the needs of the whole child so that each student has the opportunity to be healthy, safe, engaged, supported, and challenged for long-term success; and
Is monitored and reviewed through accountability systems.
School Social Workers are:
Trained mental health professionals, with a license in social work, who provide services related to student wellbeing in academics, school climate, social-emotional development, and mental health.

The link between the home, school, and community in providing direct as well as indirect services to students, families, and school personnel to promote and support students' academic and social success.
State-credentialed as defined in COMAR 13A.12.04.11.
School Social Workers shall:

Adhere to the ethics and values of the social work profession to guide ethical practice while understanding the unique aspects of school social work practice and the needs of the students, families, educational settings, and communities they serve;
Meet the provisions for professional practice of the State Department of Education and possess knowledge and understanding basic to the social work profession as well as the local school system;
Conduct assessments with the goal of improving student social, emotional, and academic learning outcomes.
Use assessment as the starting point of intervention within a multitiered system of supports;
Use data to guide service delivery and to evaluate their practice regularly to determine if services and supports need to be faded, continued, added, or increased;
Maintain accurate data and records that are relevant to assessment, planning, implementation, and evaluation of school social work services;
Organize their workloads to fulfill their responsibilities and clarify their critical roles within the educational mission of the school and county in which they work;
Use technology to enhance communication, design and deliver services, obtain, manage, and store information, and demonstrate accountability to students and families in the school setting;
Engage in professional development to provide students, families, schools, and communities with the highest-quality, culturally informed services;
Ensure that students and their families are provided services within the context of multicultural understanding and competence;
Share leadership in developing a positive school climate;
Work collaboratively with school administration, school personnel, family members, and community partners to increase accessibility to and effectiveness of all services;
Engage in advocacy that seeks to ensure that all students have equal access to education and services to enhance their academic progress;
Provide a pivotal role in creating and executing a schoolwide safety plan and provide direct and indirect services that relate to all safety concerns of students, families, and educators;
Be prepared for changes in the needs of the school community they serve and how services will be delivered when a natural disaster, (public) emergency, and/or pandemic occurs; and
Uphold the confidentiality of the students and families they serve in all formats (verbal, written, and electronic communication) according to federal, State, and local regulations and policies.

section.heading: Child Care Teachers in Preschool Centers.

para.text: To qualify or continue to qualify as a child care teacher in a preschool center, an individual shall:
Be 18 years old or older;
Have a high school diploma, a certificate of high school equivalence, or courses for credit from an accredited college or university;

Have successfully completed 6 semester hours or 90 clock hours or their equivalent of approved preservice training, or hold the Child Development Associate Credential issued by the Child Development Associate National Credentialing Program;
Have completed 3 clock hours of approved training in complying with the Americans with Disabilities Act;
Effective January 1, 2020, have completed approved basic health and safety training within 90 days of employment;
Have 9 clock hours of approved preservice training in communicating with staff, parents, and the public, or at least one academic college course for credit; and
Have at least:

1 year of experience working under supervision primarily with preschoolers in a licensed child care center, nursery school, church-operated school, or similar setting, or as a registered family child care provider caring for preschoolers; or
1 year of college, or a combination of experience and college that together are equivalent to 1 year and meet one of the criteria set forth at §A(6) of this regulation.
An individual meets the requirements of §A(3) of this regulation if the individual:
Holds an associate’s or higher degree with approved courses in early childhood education;
Has been qualified before July 1, 2008, as a child care teacher in a preschool center and has been continuously employed since that time at the same or another preschool center;
Has been approved as a teacher by the Department for early childhood in nursery school through third grade; or
Is certified by the Department or by any other state for early childhood in nursery school through third grade.
A child care teacher in a preschool center shall:

According to the individual’s professional development plan, complete approved continued training, at the rate of at least 12 clock hours per full year of employment as a child care teacher, that consists of a:
Minimum of 6 clock hours of core of knowledge training; and
Maximum of 6 clock hours of elective training;
Document completion of the continued training on the professional development plan; and
Document that the health and safety training, as required by the office, is completed by each staff member by the end of each 12-month period, measured each calendar year.
A child care teacher wishing to supervise a group of infants or toddlers shall:
Unless qualified by the office before July 1, 2008, to supervise a group of infants or toddlers:
Meet the requirements of §A of this regulation and have completed 3 semester hours of approved training, or the equivalent, related to the care of infants and toddlers; or

Meet the requirements of §A(1), (2), and (4)—(7) of this regulation and have completed 6 semester hours of approved training, or the equivalent, related exclusively to the care of infants and toddlers; and
Have completed approved training in supporting breastfeeding practices.

section.heading: Probationary Child Care Teachers in Preschool Centers.

para.text: An individual who has not met the requirements specified in Regulation .09 of this chapter is eligible for employment as a child care teacher for children 3 years old and older in a preschool center for a probationary period of up to 6 months if the individual:
Is applying for employment as a child care teacher for the first time in a Maryland center or home;
Is 18 years old or older;
Is enrolled in 3 clock hours of approved training in compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act;
Is enrolled in the approved basic health and safety training; and
Meets the requirements of §B or C of this regulation.
An individual meets the requirements of §A(5) of this regulation, if the individual:
Holds an associate degree or a bachelor’s degree in:
Early childhood education;
Elementary education;
Child development;
Home economics;
Nursing;
Social work;
Special education; or
A related field approved by the Department; and
Is enrolled in 90 clock hours or 6 semester hours of approved preservice training.
An individual meets the requirements of §A(5) of this regulation, if the individual:
Holds an associate degree or a bachelor’s degree in a field other than the fields specified in §B(1) of this regulation;
Has successfully completed at least 45 clock hours of the 90 clock hours or 3 semester hours of the 6 semester hours of approved preservice training; and
Is enrolled in the remaining 45 clock hours or 3 semester hours of the approved preservice training.
A probationary employee shall complete:
The approved basic health and safety training required in §A(4) of this regulation within 90 days of employment;
The approved training in compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act as required in §A(3) of this regulation within 6 months of employment; and
The approved preservice training required in §B(2) or C(3) of this regulation within 6 months of employment.

Except as provided in §F of this regulation, if a probationary employee fails to complete any of the training requirements of this regulation within the time periods designated in §D of this regulation, a preschool center shall either terminate the probationary employee or reassign the probationary employee to a non-teaching position at the center.
If a preschool center requests an extension of time for a probationary employee to complete any of the training requirements of this regulation, the Department may:

Without further cause, deny the request and direct the preschool center to either terminate the probationary employee or reassign the probationary employee to a non-teaching position at the center; or

Upon a showing of good cause, grant the request and allow the probationary teacher to remain in a teaching position at the center for a period of time determined by the Department and approved by the Superintendent.

section.heading: Child Care Teachers in School Age Centers.

1 year of college; or
A combination of experience and college that together are equivalent to 1 year;

Early childhood education, elementary education, special education, or child development; or

para.text: A family child care teacher in a child care home shall be 18 years old or older.
To qualify or continue to qualify as a family child care teacher, an individual:
Shall hold or have successfully completed:
A high school diploma, a certificate of high school equivalence, or courses for credit from an accredited college or university;
9 clock hours of approved preservice training in communicating with staff, parents, and the public or at least one academic college course for credit;
Approved preservice training in child development and curriculum documented by:
6 semester hours or 90 clock hours or their equivalent;
The Child Development Associate Credential issued by the Child Development Associate National Credentialing Program; or
Accreditation by the National Association for Family Child Care as a family child care provider;
3 clock hours of approved training in complying with the Americans with Disabilities Act; and
Effective January 1, 2020, approved basic health and safety training within 90 days of employment; and
Shall have completed at least one of the following:
1 year of experience working under supervision with children in licensed child care center, nursery school, church-operated school, or similar setting;
1 year of experience as a registered family child care provider; or
1 year of college, or a combination of experience and college that together are equivalent to 1 year.
An individual shall qualify as a family child care teacher if the individual has met the requirements of §B of this regulation and:
Holds an associate's or higher degree with approved courses in early childhood education;
Qualified before July 1, 2008, as a child care teacher in a licensed child care center and has been continuously employed since that time at the same or another licensed child care center;
Has been approved as a teacher by the Department for early childhood in nursery school through third grade; or
Is certified by the Department or by any other state for early childhood in nursery school through third grade.
A family child care teacher in a child care home shall:

According to the individual's professional development plan, complete approved continued training, at the rate of at least 12 clock hours per full year of employment as a child care teacher, that consists of a:
Minimum of 6 clock hours of core of knowledge training; and
Maximum of 6 clock hours of elective training;
Document completion of the continued training on the professional development plan; and
Document that the health and safety training, as required by the office, is completed by each staff member by the end of each 12-month period, measured each calendar year.
Before a family child care teacher may supervise a child younger than 2 years old, the individual shall:
Effective January 1, 2016, complete approved training in supporting breastfeeding practices; and
Unless previously qualified by the office to supervise an infant or a toddler:
Meet the requirements of §§A and B of this regulation and have completed 3 semester hours of approved training, or the equivalent, related to the care of children younger than 2 years old; or
Be 18 years old or older and:
Meet the requirements of §B(1)(a), (b), (d), (e), and (2) of this regulation; and
Have completed 6 semester hours of approved training, or the equivalent, related to the care of children younger than 2 years old.

An individual who has not met the requirements specified in Regulation .06 of this chapter is eligible for employment as a family child care teacher for children 3 years old and older in a child care home for a probationary period of up to 6 months if the individual:
Is applying for employment as a family child care teacher for the first time in a Maryland center or home;
Is 18 years old or older;
Is enrolled in 3 clock hours of approved training in compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act;
Is enrolled in the approved basic health and safety training; and
Meets the requirements of §B or C of this regulation.
An individual meets the requirements of §A(5) of this regulation, if the individual:
Holds an associate degree or a bachelor’s degree in:
Early childhood education;
Elementary education;
Child development;
Home economics;
Nursing;
Social work;
Special education; or
A related field approved by the Department; and
Is enrolled in a 90-hour or 6 semester hours of approved preservice training.
An individual meets the requirements of §A(5) of this regulation, if the individual:
Holds an associate degree or a bachelor’s degree in a field other than the fields specified in §B(1) of this regulation;
Has successfully completed at least 45 clock hours of the 90 clock hours or 3 semester hours of the 6 semester hours of approved preservice training; and
Is enrolled in the remaining 45 clock hours or 3 semester hours of the approved preservice training.
A probationary employee shall complete:
The approved basic health and safety training required in §A(4) of this regulation within 90 days of employment;
The approved training in compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act as required in §A(3) of this regulation within 6 months of employment; and
The approved preservice training required in §B(2) or C(3) of this regulation within 6 months of employment.

Except as provided in §F of this regulation, if a probationary employee fails to complete any of the training requirements of this regulation within the time periods designated in §D of this regulation, a family child care home shall either terminate the probationary employee or reassign the probationary employee to a non-teaching position at the child care home.
If a family child care home requests an extension of time for a probationary employee to complete any of the training requirements of this regulation, the Department may:

Without further cause, deny the request and direct the family child care home to either terminate the probationary employee or reassign the probationary employee to a non-teaching position at the child care home; or

Upon a showing of good cause, grant the request and allow the probationary teacher to remain in a teaching position at the child care home for a period of time determined by the Department and approved by the Superintendent.

section.heading: Purpose.
section.text: The Attendant Care Program provides financial reimbursement to assist individuals with severe chronic or permanent physical disabilities who require attendant care services or ongoing additional supports to direct their own care and select their own service providers. Reimbursement may be available for attendant care services or ongoing additional supports that are provided in the home, school, workplace, or other community locations.

para.text: In this chapter, the following terms have the meanings indicated.
Terms Defined.
“Annual adjusted gross income” means the total taxable and nontaxable annual income, less 100 percent of total unreimbursed medical expenses as defined by COMAR 07.03.17.33, of:
The eligible applicant; and
The applicant's spouse.
“Applicant” means an individual who has submitted an application to participate in the Program in order to receive reimbursement of the cost of attendant care services or ongoing additional supports.
“Attendant” means an individual or provider agency who provides attendant care services to a participant.
“Attendant care agreement” means a written agreement developed by the Department that:
Provides:
The effective date for reimbursable services; and
The terms for reimbursement under the Program; and
Is signed by the participant and the Program Director at the time of initial enrollment and at the request of the Program Director if any circumstances change for the individual or the program.

“Attendant care services” means any of the following services for an individual, which are deemed necessary by an attending physician or by a registered nurse or certified nurse practitioner serving the individual including:
Activities of daily living such as:
Dressing;
Preparing food and assisting with eating;
Bathing and personal hygiene;
Assisting with routine bodily functions, including bowel and urinary care; and
Moving into, out of, or turning in bed; or
Instrumental activities of daily living such as:
Laundering and other clothing care;
Cleaning house; and
Performing other services of daily care, including shopping and transportation.
“Attending physician” means an individual who is authorized to practice medicine in this State and who has provided medical treatment to an applicant.
“Certification of service form” means a document designated by the Department that verifies the participant's receipt of attendant care services for billing purposes.
“Department” means the Department of Disabilities.

“Duplicative services” means comparable care services or ongoing additional supports provided through any other federal or State assistance programs, such as but not limited to the programs described in COMAR 07.06.12, 10.09.04, or 10.09.20.
“Episodic” means when an impairment or medical condition varies in frequency, intensity and duration and renders the person unable to engage in major life activities when onset.
“Financial assistance” means reimbursement by the Department of the eligible percentage of the cost paid by a participant for attendant care services or ongoing additional supports.

“Fiscal payment schedule” means the list of 12 1-month periods, established annually by the Program Director, in which Attendant Care Program benefits are provided, and participants are required to submit certification of service forms and receipts for reimbursement processing.
“Home visit” means a visit by the Program Director or designee to the home of the Program participant.

“Ongoing additional supports” means a continual support that increases an eligible individual’s independent performance of an essential activity of daily living, self-care, or mobility, and is requested by a Participant and approved by the Department.
“Participant” means an eligible and enrolled individual in the Program.

“Permanent physical disability” means a medical condition that substantially affects an individual's ability to perform physical activities such as walking, standing, transferring, seeing, or hearing.
“Program” means the Attendant Care Program.
“Program Director” means the individual designated by the Secretary to oversee the day-to-day operations of the Program.

“Review of financial or programmatic eligibility” means initiating verification that the participant remains eligible within 1 calendar year since the completion of the most recent review or more frequently if requested by the Department or the individual.

“Severe chronic disability” means a recurring medical condition that substantially limits an individual's mobility or ability to perform activities of daily living, instrumental activities of daily living, or self-care:
Permanently; or
On an ongoing basis or episodically, as defined by Regulation .02B(10) of this chapter.
“Sliding reimbursement scale” means the percentage breakdown of maximum financial assistance afforded to a Program participant based upon adjusted gross income and household size.
“Standard assessment of functional capability” means the document designated by the Department to evaluate an applicant's:
Ability to perform essential activities of daily living and self-care;
Mobility;
Need for assistance with instrumental activities of daily living; and
Need for attendant care services or ongoing additional supports.
“Receipts” means proof of payment made for an approved service designated by the Department.
To be eligible for the Program, an applicant:
Shall be a resident of Maryland;
Shall be at least 18 years old and younger than 65 years old at the time of initial enrollment in the Program;
Shall be determined by the applicant's attending physician, registered nurse, or certified nurse practitioner to have a severe chronic or permanent physical disability that:

Precludes or impairs the independent performance of essential activities of daily living, instrumental activities of daily living, self-care, or mobility as determined by the standard assessment of functional capability form; and
Is subject to eligibility review at a frequency determined by the Department;
May not have an annual adjusted gross income greater than $119,999;
May not be receiving duplicative services as defined in Regulation .02B of this chapter;
Shall meet the requirements of Regulation .04B(1) or (2) of this chapter; and

Shall agree to abide by the Program requirements by signing an attendant care agreement form at the time of initial enrollment and at the request of the Program Director if any circumstances change for the individual or the Program.

The Program Director, or designee, shall initiate an annual review of financial or programmatic eligibility for each participant at least once every 12 months from completion of the last review, or more frequently if needed.
Participation in the Program may be denied to eligible applicants in accordance with Regulation .04 of this chapter.

section.heading: Limitations on Service and Participation in the Program.

para.text: The Program Director shall limit Program participation to the number of participants whom the Program's budget can serve. If sufficient funds are not available, the Department may limit the rate of payment under the sliding reimbursement scale.
The Program Director shall limit Program participation to achieve the following demographic:
At least 50 percent of the participants shall be:
Self-employed or competitively employed with compensation;

Actively seeking employment and reasonably be expected to become employed within 6 months of the date of application approval, which the Program Director may extend once for an additional 6 months; or
Attending an institution of postsecondary, higher education, or apprenticeship training program; and
Not more than 50 percent of the participants shall be:
At risk of placement in a nursing home, as certified by the attending physician, if attendant care services are not received in the community; or
Residents of a nursing facility or similar institution who are seeking to transition into the community and will be capable of living in the community if attendant care services are received.
The Program Director shall seek to achieve the demographic in §B absent a limited or situational waiver from the Secretary.
Notwithstanding the above, an applicant found ineligible or properly disenrolled from the Program shall be required to observe a waiting period prior to reapplication of not less than:
One year for reason of disability or financial eligibility; or
Three years upon a finding of fraud or misuse of program funds.
Applicants to the Program shall be encouraged to complete an application for medical assistance and utilize personal care services under the following programs, if applicable:
Examples of such services or programs include:
Community Personal Assistance Services;
Community First Choice Program; or
A Home and Community-Based Waiver.
The Program is entitled to evaluate whether such services are duplicative.
An applicant shall apply for financial assistance by submitting a completed and signed Program application, to include the standard assessment of functional capability, to the Department.
The Program Director or designee shall determine an applicant's eligibility in accordance with Regulation .03 of this chapter and the regulations governing this Program as a whole.
The Program Director shall approve applications and enroll eligible applicants for financial assistance based upon the availability of Program funds.
Waiting List.
The Program Director shall establish a waiting list of eligible applicants if:
Program funds are not available; or
The demographics of the Program do not meet the requirements under Regulation .04B of this chapter.
As funds allow, the Program shall enroll applicants on the waiting list generally in the following order:
Individuals meeting the criteria under Regulation .04B(1) of this chapter in order of the earlier application approval date; and
Individuals meeting the criteria under Regulation .04B(2) of this chapter in order of the earlier application approval date.

With the explicit written consent of the Secretary, and after obtaining a waiver of the proportionality requirement set forth in Regulation .04B(1) of this chapter as necessary, in limited emergency circumstances, the Program Director may prioritize certain individuals meeting the criteria under Regulation .04B(2)(a) of this chapter before other individuals meeting the criteria under .04B(2)(a) of this chapter.
A participant shall submit a signed certification of service form and receipts for attendant care services or ongoing additional supports in accordance with the Program's fiscal payment schedule.
Reimbursement shall be made in compliance with the attendant care agreement and Regulation .04A of this chapter.
The Department may return improperly completed forms to the participant without making payment.
The Department may return the certification of service form to the participant without making payment if more than 2 months have passed since the date of service.
The Department reserves the right to deny reimbursement of expenses that it determines are not representative of ongoing additional supports or attendant care services.
A participant shall:
Select, hire, train, supervise, terminate, and pay the attendant, including payment of applicable federal and State employment taxes;
Maintain accurate records of hours and days that attendant care services are provided;
Prepare and submit all billing forms in accordance with the Fiscal Payment Schedule;
Reimburse the Department for any overpayment;
Reimburse the Department for any outstanding advanced payment;
Submit all required documentation to determine continued eligibility for participation in the Program at least once every 12 months, or more often as requested by the Program Director; and

Comply with the attendant care agreement requirements, and provide a signed copy to the Department at the initial eligibility determination and at the request of the Department at any time thereafter.
A participant shall employ an attendant who is 18 years old or older, and who is not a spouse or the representative payee of the participant.
A participant shall notify the Program Director within 14 days of any changes in circumstances that affect eligibility for the Program for financial assistance.

section.heading: Participant's Rights.
section.text: Pursuant to Human Services Article, §1-201, Annotated Code of Maryland, the Program may not release information about a participant or an applicant.

para.text: The Department shall establish a quality assurance plan to review Program administration and ensure compliance with this chapter.
Home visits may be conducted as a part of the quality assurance plan.

section.heading: Termination.
section.text: The Secretary of the Department or a designee of the Secretary may terminate enrollment if:

para.text: A participant no longer meets the eligibility requirements;
A participant refuses to comply with the requirements of this chapter; or
Sufficient Program funds are not available.
The Program Director shall establish a sliding reimbursement scale to determine a participant's reimbursement rate.
The participant's reimbursement rate shall be based on:
The participant's adjusted annual gross income;
The number of persons dependent on household income including the participant's spouse, and minors younger than 18 years old; and
The participant's cost of attendant care services.

A participant eligible in the category set forth in Regulation .04B(1) of this chapter shall pay a minimum of 2 percent of the cost of attendant care services, unless the Program Director determines that the minimum copayment causes the participant financial hardship and issues a written waiver of the copayment.

A participant eligible in the category set forth in Regulation .04B(2) of this chapter shall pay a minimum of 5 percent of the cost of attendant care services, unless the Program Director determines that the minimum copayment causes the participant financial hardship and issues a written waiver of the copayment.
An applicant or participant may appeal eligibility and termination determinations by requesting an appeal hearing which shall be held in accordance with COMAR 28.02.01.

If the Program notifies an applicant or participant of an action to deny, delay, suspend, reduce, or terminate assistance, the Program Director or designee shall give written notification of the right to appeal and the procedures for requesting an appeal hearing to the applicant or participant.

para.text: If a Maryland offense has not been assigned a seriousness category and the offense has a maximum penalty of 1 year or less, the offense shall be assigned the lowest seriousness category (VII).

If a Maryland offense has not been assigned a seriousness category and the offense has a maximum penalty greater than 1 year, the individual completing the worksheet shall use the closest analogous offense and the sentencing judge and parties shall be notified.

For Prior Record calculations involving an out of jurisdiction adjudication, the individual completing the worksheet shall match the offense as closely as possible to the closest analogous Maryland offense. If no Maryland analogous offense exists, the individual completing the worksheet shall count the offense in the lowest seriousness category (VII), and shall inform the judge and parties. If the out of jurisdiction adjudication is based on an act that is not a criminal violation in Maryland (e.g., cannabis possession), then the out of jurisdiction adjudication shall be excluded from the prior adult criminal record. If there is a question as to the analogous guidelines offense for an out-of-State adjudication, that question should be brought to the attention of the judge at sentencing.

para.text: Performance Bonds.

General. A performance bond is required for all construction contracts in excess of the applicable small procurement amount in COMAR 21.05.07.01 in the amount equal to at least 100 percent of the contract price. A performance bond may be required for a contract for services, supplies, maintenance, or construction-related services expected to exceed the applicable small procurement amount in COMAR 21.05.07.01, as determined by the procurement officer. The performance bond shall be delivered by the contractor to the State not later than the time the contract is executed. If a contractor fails to deliver the required performance bond, the contractor’s bid shall be rejected, its bid security shall be enforced, and award of the contract may be made to the next lowest responsive and responsible bidder.

Reduction of Amount Before Solicitation. The head of a procurement agency may reduce the amount of the performance bond required before solicitation if, after completing appropriate analysis, it is determined in writing by the head of a procurement agency to be less costly or more advantageous to the State to self-insure a part of the performance of the contractor. An analysis may be made for groups of contracts, or may be made on particular contracts, as the head of a procurement agency chooses. A copy of the analysis shall be available for public inspection.
Payment Bonds.

General. A payment bond is required for all construction contracts in excess of the applicable small procurement amount in COMAR 21.05.07.01 in the amount equal to at least 100 percent of the contract price. A payment bond may be required for a contract for services, supplies, maintenance, or construction-related services expected to exceed the applicable small procurement amount in COMAR 21.05.07.01, as determined by the procurement officer. The payment bond shall be delivered by the contractor to the State not later than the time the contract is executed. If a contractor fails to deliver the required payment bond, the contractor's bid shall be rejected, its bid security shall be enforced, and award of the contract shall be made to the next lowest responsive and responsible bidder.

Reduction of Amount Before Solicitation. Before solicitation, the head of a procurement agency may reduce the amount of the payment bond to not less than 50 percent of the contract price if a written determination is made that it is in the best interest of the State to do so. Factors to be considered in order to make the determination include, but are not limited to:
The value and number of subcontracts to be awarded by the contractor; and
The value of the contract.
Forms for Performance and Payment Bonds. The required performance and payment bonds shall be in the form specified in COMAR 21.07.02.10.
